lesson.subject: anatomy
lesson.title: Pancreas and its duct relationships
lesson.summary: Use the neck as the reference plane.

steps.title: Pancreas
steps.body: The pancreas is a mostly secondarily retroperitoneal foregut organ behind the stomach and related to the C-loop of duodenum and splenic vessels. It has head, uncinate process, neck, body, and tail.

steps.title: Relationships and functional organization
steps.body: Head lies in the duodenal curve. Uncinate process extends posterior to superior mesenteric vessels. Neck lies anterior to formation of portal vein. Body crosses toward the spleen; splenic artery runs along superior border and splenic vein posterior to the pancreas. Tail reaches the splenic hilum in the splenorenal ligament region.

steps.title: How do the pancreatic duct and arterial patterns fit its position?
steps.body: The main duct generally runs from tail toward head and joins the bile-duct outlet region; an accessory duct may open separately at the minor papilla. Pancreaticoduodenal arcades supply the head around the duodenal curve, while branches of the splenic artery supply much of body and tail. Thus the organ spans linked arterial territories and a longitudinal drainage route. Endocrine secretions enter blood directly, whereas exocrine secretions use ducts; those two outputs should not be drawn as one pathway.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: Use the neck as the reference plane. The superior mesenteric and splenic veins unite behind it; the uncinate process projects behind the superior mesenteric vessels. Farther left, the splenic vein lies posterior to the body and the splenic artery runs along its superior border. The tail enters the splenorenal ligament toward the splenic hilum. These distinctions explain why pancreatic, splenic and portal anatomy must be learned together rather than as isolated organ lists.
